summary: Comments on the File Transfer Protocol, proposing design changes and slight modifications. It replaces the earlier discussion in RFC 607 and is related to RFCs 614, 542 and 640.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC lists proposed changes to make FTP easier to implement. It replaces a draft that had been released while still in rough form.

questions: what is the actv ftp command
why does ftp use reply codes
subtitle: Lists proposed fixes for implementation problems in the File Transfer Protocol.

tldr.problem: The FTP protocol described in RFC 542 had ambiguities and design choices that the authors said complicated user and server implementations.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 624 presents twelve problems and proposed solutions involving command verbs, transfer handshakes, reply codes, line lengths and reply nesting.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 607, a rough draft released inadvertently; the RFC presents proposals rather than a revised protocol specification.

today: RFC 624 obsoletes RFC 607. It is a set of comments and proposed solutions, not a replacement FTP specification.

sections.title: Comments on RFC 542
sections.content:
RFC 624 replaces RFC 607, which the authors say was released inadvertently while still in rough draft form. They ask readers to disregard that earlier document and treat RFC 624 as the accurate statement of their opinions.

The authors distinguish basic protocol drawbacks that would require substantial design changes from issues they believe could be remedied with little effort. This memo lists the latter with proposed solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors correct a mistakenly released draft. They then list changes they believe could be made with little effort.

sections.title: Commands and Transfer Handshakes
sections.content:
The proposals include an ACTV command to make a passive server active without the extra effects of REIN, replacing the three-letter BYE command with a four-letter verb such as QUIT, and requiring command verbs to have four letters.

For transfer setup, the authors propose that the server send the 250 reply before attempting to establish the data connection. They also propose that unsupported-but-unneeded commands receive a success reply and that limits be set for command lines, replies, user names, passwords, accounts and pathnames.
sections.plainLanguage: The suggestions make command lengths consistent and clarify the order of the server's reply and data connection setup. The authors also ask for defined maximum lengths.

sections.title: Reply Codes and Continuation Lines
sections.content:
The authors say multi-line replies with arbitrary continuation text and nesting make FTP clients harder to implement. They propose a unique numeric code, such as 009, for continuation lines, or otherwise limiting or disallowing nested replies.

They also note that successful commands can return codes with different first digits. They propose a shared success digit, clearer descriptions for reply codes and more consistent connection greeting codes. The final item notes that 332 LOGIN PLEASE is missing from the command-reply table.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposals aim to make replies easier for programs to interpret. The authors want success and continuation replies to follow clearer patterns.

references.text: "Comments on the File Transfer Protocol", RFC 607, replaced by RFC 624.
